Then I resolved to pour out My fury upon them, to vent all My anger upon them there, in the land of Egypt.’ Context and connection to Ohr Zarua LaTzadik: In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Large Aleph; Small Aleph, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Ezekiel 20:8) to illuminate his exposition here (“And through this we can understand why at times superfluous Alephs are found appended, as in: eshkar ("they shall bring presents" [Psalms 72:10]), ve-he'eznichu ("and the rivers shall become foul" [Isaiah 19:6]),...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the hidden light of Torah, the spiritual root of the letters and mitzvot, and the halakhic-aggadic synthesis developed in Ohr Zarua LaTzadik.
column13: This dispute dates to antiquity, and the Gemara resolves it: "This is for us [in Babylonia], and that is for them [in the Land of Israel]": as written in Nedarim (22a): "a trembling heart" is said regarding the exile in Babylonia, where the heart is agitated and dominates man, leaving his heart outside his sovereign control (unlike the righteous whose heart is in their hands), owing to the coarseness of the Babylonian exile; for such a person, he must marry a wife first to purge bodily temptation.

column15: And he sent forth a raven, and it went forth to and fro, etc. Raven alludes to anger, and Noah desired that the trait of anger not be found in the world, and the Holy One, blessed be He, showed him that for the time being there is still a necessity for this trait in the world; for sometimes, counter to desire when some evil lust confronts a person, he can save himself through working himself into anger; and this is the explanation of 'and it went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up': meaning until corrupt desires cease from the world, then anger too shall be nullified, for water signifies desire.

column13: For the holiness of the Land consists in this: that he possesses a God, as written in Ketubot 110b, and licentiousness causes this awareness to be forgotten, as written in the Zohar Vayishlach, Part I, 163b on the displaced sinew Gid HaNasheh—an expression of displacement and forgetfulness, its inner meaning being the corruption of the holy Covenant; and as they said in Sotah 9a: “He acted as though the supernal Eye does not see, etc.”, countering what is written of the Land of Israel: “the eyes of Hashem your God are always upon it.”

column15: Prior to creation existence was like a wilderness, where divine providence was not overtly discerned, for before creation Hashem was termed “He” (Hu). And likewise in the Wilderness Generation, who clarified through faith that even in the barren desert Hashem sustains life, and through this acquired the Land of Israel, concerning which it is written (Deuteronomy 11:12): “A land which the Lord your God cares for continually”—where it is visibly manifest that Hashem sustains, and He is addressed directly as “You” (Attah).
